At 9.20 on Wednesday morning, 900 children were halfway through the early shift at Tribhuvan Trishuli secondary school, a three-storey complex in the Trishuli valley of north-central Nepal.⁠ ⁠ Another 700 were on their way on foot and by bus, when the principal, Rajendra Dadabi, received a panicked call from a friend in Betrawati, five miles upstream. “He said the village was gone: taken by the river,” said Dadabi. “He told me to run.”⁠ ⁠ The 47-year-old English teacher took a moment to consider the threat. He remembered that the school buses, each carrying 80 children, were en route.⁠ ⁠ “I got through to all the drivers but one and told them to turn back. Then I saw the bus I hadn’t been able to contact coming across the bridge. By now, the water was in the school grounds — it was so fast — so I told him to turn around. It got to the other side just as the bridge collapsed.”⁠ ⁠ Dadabi’s quick thinking saved the lives of 1,643 children and all but one member of the teaching staff. #nepal #nepalfloods #floods

Uma família tenta se abrigar em uma casa, enquanto o mar de lama varre várias outras, imagens impressionantes. Cientistas e imagens de satélite confirmam: não foi terremoto. Foi o colapso de parte de uma geleira lá em cima, perto do pico Langtang Lirung, a mais de 5 mil metros. Um bloco enorme de gelo e rocha desceu cerca de 1.200 metros, bloqueou temporariamente o rio e, quando a barreira cedeu, gerou aquela onda gigante de água, lama e detritos. O impacto foi tão forte que registrou magnitude 5.2 nos sensores. Em 30 minutos o nível do rio subiu vários metros. Algumas pessoas nas redes ligam o evento a profecias antigas. A ciência, porém, aponta para um processo natural de instabilidade da geleira, possivelmente influenciado pelo aquecimento na região. More than 1,300 people are missing in Nepal and Tibet, including 47 Americans, after a glacial collapse caused catastrophic floods, with video showing mud sweeping through entire communities. Drone footage in Nepal showed roads destroyed and buildings buried by thundering water the color of wet cement. Nepalese authorities ramped up operations in the worst-affected districts of Nuwakot and Rasuwa. The disaster in Nepal and Tibet is not a one-off. The Lhende Khola river system has now flooded twice in just 14 months and the increasingly unstable Himalayan ice system threatens communities, infrastructure and water supplies across one of the world’s most densely populated regions. The region saw similar flash floods in August last year, when a glacial lake in Tibet overflowed because of high temperatures. Nine people were killed, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting Nepal and China, was damaged.

🇳🇵 LOCAL SURVIVORS OF THE NEPAL FLOODS: THEY SURVIVED, BUT LOST ALMOST EVERYTHING For many local people, surviving the devastating floods was only the beginning of another struggle. 73-year-old Bhakta Lal Shrestha was at an elderly home in Devighat when the flood struck. He and more than 100 other residents were trapped for nearly nine hours before rescuers finally reached them. In Tupche village, 49-year-old Parbati Adhikari survived because she had left her village to visit a nearby temple before the flood arrived. When she tried to return, five bridges had already been washed away. She eventually found shelter with other survivors and was reunited with her husband and son. And 8-year-old Zoyal Ghale survived by running into the forest and climbing trees as floodwaters tore through his community. Injured and alone, he was eventually rescued and later reunited with his mother. These are more than numbers. They are mothers, fathers, children, grandparents and entire families who watched their homes disappear in minutes. Some survived. Some are still missing. And thousands of survivors are now facing the painful question: “Where do we go from here?” 🇳🇵💔 #NepalFloods #Nepal #FloodSurvivors #SurvivalStory #RescueMission
